title: Gibraltar's Chief Minister on the UK-EU Treaty: Sovereignty, Borders, and Business
label: 15 September 2026 · Gibraltar treaty evidence
summary: The European Affairs Committee questioned Fabian Picardo, Chief Minister of Gibraltar, about the UK-EU agreement on Gibraltar. He explained why Gibraltar voted 96% to stay in the EU in 2016, how the treaty protects sovereignty while ensuring fluidity at the border, the role of the European Court of Justice, new immigration and residency rules, tax governance, financial contributions, and the practical teething problems since provisional application began on 15 July. He argued the treaty is imperfect but necessary, and confirmed that Gibraltar's sovereignty remains exclusively British.

chapters.title: Why Gibraltar voted 96% to stay in the EU
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar feared Brexit would wreck its economy and border fluidity, so it voted overwhelmingly to remain.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Chief Minister. Let's start with the big picture: why did Gibraltar vote so overwhelmingly to stay in the EU, and why has it taken so long to get this treaty?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: 2016 was very difficult for us. The result upended our economy and threatened the ability of many Gibraltarians to visit family in Spain or simply live the lives we live with access to southern Spain and Europe.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: We have 15,000 people crossing into Gibraltar every day. New EU border rules would have made that much harder. Voters understood that without needing it explained.

turns.speaker: Baroness Suttie
turns.text: Which practical problems were most difficult, and will the treaty fix them?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Frontier fluidity was the starkest and most dangerous issue. Cross-border workers keep our public services, health care, elderly care, gaming and insurance industries running. If they can't get in smoothly, our public services and public finances are at risk.

chapters.title: Did the change of UK government matter?
chapters.takeaway: Both UK parties supported Gibraltar, but global geopolitics gave the talks a bigger push than the 2024 election.

turns.speaker: The Duke of Wellington
turns.text: When the UK government changed in 2024, did that affect the tone, speed or ease of negotiations?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Both UK parties have been equally supportive, through the withdrawal agreement, the New Year's Eve framework and this treaty. I accompanied Lord Cameron and later David Lammy and Stephen Doughty.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: A Labour government in Madrid gave a bit of ideological hope, but if I'm honest, President Trump and Vice-President Vance's Munich speech in February 2025 gave the biggest boost. Europe and the UK realised they needed to work together, not fight over two and a half square miles.

chapters.title: Sovereignty and the European Court of Justice
chapters.takeaway: Picardo insists Gibraltar's sovereignty is untouched and that ECJ involvement is only about consistent interpretation of shared rules, not sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Baroness Smith of Newnham
turns.text: The 2021 principles said sovereignty over Gibraltar wouldn't pass to another state without your consent. Have those aims been achieved?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Those were my aims, not the Foreign Secretary's. The double lock on our 2006 constitution is a sine qua non. Every UK Foreign Secretary has accepted that exclusively British sovereignty cannot be compromised by one iota. It hasn't been.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: Does the European Court of Justice's role in interpreting EU law threaten Gibraltar's sovereignty in future?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Absolutely not. Gibraltar voted 96% to remain, with full ECJ jurisdiction. We're like the UK in 1972 agreeing to abide by a club's rules. The ECJ can only tell us what European text means. That's jurisprudential consistency, not sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: You can't have the same words interpreted differently in the same circumstances. A directive on the environment can't mean one thing in the EU and another under our treaty. That's why the ECJ's interpretation matters.

chapters.title: Who gets in and who gets refused
chapters.takeaway: Border refusals work through consecutive Gibraltar and Schengen checks, with no single-refusal cases so far.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: How does the agreement deal with refusing individual entry? Who decides, and when?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: It's complex, but the principle is simple. Gibraltar keeps its own immigration check and Schengen does its own. If Gibraltar allows you in but Schengen refuses, you can only visit Gibraltar. If Gibraltar refuses you but Schengen allows you, you can enter Schengen through a different exit at the airport.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: So it's exit but not via the gift shop?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Exactly. And if someone is refused by Gibraltar but allowed into Schengen, we put their face in our facial recognition system. If they enter Gibraltar, they're here illegally.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How do you know they don't cross into Spain if the border is fluid?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: They could come into Gibraltar but would be in Spain illegally if they crossed. It's like Germany letting you in without a Schengen visa—you can't legally go to France. In the two months of these arrangements, we've had no such single-refusal cases.

chapters.title: Tax, jobs and money
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar already meets top tax transparency standards, will fund a cohesion mechanism itself, and says new residency rules aren't required by the treaty.

turns.speaker: Lord Grantchester
turns.text: How will the treaty's tax governance obligations work, and what do they mean for Gibraltar's tax policy?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: We already align completely with OECD best practice. We were the first EU jurisdiction to implement an open register of beneficial ownership, ahead of the UK, Germany and France. We signed up with no objection. It doesn't stop us being a competitive, well-regulated financial centre.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: With the old UK visa route ending, are businesses worried they'll hire young Spanish people instead of young British people who used to come to Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: I'm sorry, but that's a misconceived approach. There are almost none of those young Brits in our job market. We have seven unemployed residents—not 7%, seven people. 15,500 cross-border workers come daily, half Spanish, half from the balance of British and others. They'll continue to come.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: New residence requirements are our own sovereign decision, not a treaty requirement. We set a minimum earnings threshold of around £37,000 because the treaty makes Gibraltar more attractive as a place to live. We have exemptions for young people and want digital talent from any nationality.

turns.speaker: Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell
turns.text: How much will Gibraltar pay into the financial mechanism, and will the UK contribute?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Gibraltar will contribute, not the UK taxpayer. We'll raise it from our own taxpayers and companies. It'll be used to train people for the Gibraltar job market. It'll start in the low millions.

chapters.title: Gibraltar's parliament, the concordat and provisional application
chapters.takeaway: The treaty was endorsed unanimously in Gibraltar, the concordat clarifies responsibilities, and provisional application since 15 July has shown the treaty working despite teething problems.

turns.speaker: Lord Barrow
turns.text: The agreement was unanimously endorsed by Gibraltar's parliament. What was welcomed, and were there hidden concerns? And how do you see the concordat with the UK?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Opposition concerns are on the record. This is a compromise between the UK, EU, Spain and Gibraltar. I've called it imperfect but exactly what we need to keep going with our sovereignty intact. The opposition leader used the same words last week. The concordat sets out who does what and who pays for what. It's been scrutinised and found satisfactory, if not perfect.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ashton of Upholland
turns.text: Why did you have to provisionally apply the treaty from 15 July rather than fully apply it? Has anything emerged during this period?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: We had to avoid the new EU entry and exit system causing huge tailbacks at the frontier. We couldn't ratify in time, so we included a provisional application clause, suggested by the Commission. Ratification is expected at the Strasbourg session on 14 or 15 December.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: During provisional application, airport delays are shorter than at larger European airports. We had some customs traffic issues early on—a regional fair blocked lorry turnaround—but things are working. Truck numbers dropped from 250–300 a day to 100–150, but we're back up now. We're finessing the sticky bits.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: Have you published guidance on the new residency regulations?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Yes. I'll write to you with the date and the regulations.

chapters.title: Trade, AI rules and the future
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar is a services economy that can still join services parts of trade deals like CPTPP, but accepts compromises on goods and some EU regulations to keep border fluidity.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: British people on the Costa del Sol used to bank in Gibraltar. Is that still common, and does the treaty help them?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: That's no longer a discernible part of our business. Banks here don't offer banking to non-residents. People in the Costas bank in Spain or the UK. We see tourists and expats shopping, not banking.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: Do you expect this agreement to settle matters for the foreseeable future, or will more agreements be needed?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: On fluidity, it's settled. There may be rhetoric in a Spanish election year, but the arrangements give business efficacy. Sovereignty is unchanged for the UK and Spain. We still fight for self-determination in New York, where we remain on the non-self-governing territories list.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: You heard a previous witness say Gibraltar can't join the CPTPP in goods. Will you be controlled by EU product rules like the AI Act or Cyber Resilience Act? Would that make you more like an EU overseas territory?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: We're physically attached to Europe, so people and goods need to flow. But we never agreed to free movement of people—just fluidity. We can have all the UK's trade agreements extended to us in services, which is where our business is. We can't grow goods in 2.5 square miles.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: On AI and cyber, we're as free as the UK unless there's a grey area around goods and services. We've chosen to compromise on things like GM food research we never had, to keep growing in services. We hope the UK's reset with the EU includes an SPS agreement so British produce can come here.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: That would be tragic for our economy.

chapters.title: Farewell
chapters.takeaway: Picardo thanked the committee and announced he will retire as Chief Minister in the coming months.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Chief Minister. This has been most helpful for the House's consideration of the treaty.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: May I say something before you close? I want to thank you and earlier configurations of this committee for your interest in Gibraltar. I'll be retiring from office in the coming months, so this is likely my last appearance. Thank you for all your considerations over the past decade and a half.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We wish you a happy, productive and busy retirement. Thank you very much.
